incidents.name: Na Lao irrigation weir
incidents.location_label: Santi Suk, Nan Province, Thailand
incidents.river_or_facility: Na Lao irrigation weir
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain and strong currents washed away one side of the Na Lao irrigation weir and damaged the adjacent road.
incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain across Nan Province on 19 August 2026 damaged irrigation and road infrastructure. Khaosod English, citing the Nan provincial public relations office, reported that strong currents washed away one side of the Na Lao irrigation weir in Santi Suk district and damaged the road beside it. The same storm cut the Phayaeng–Kiew Muang approach to the provincial capital, stranded people on a Muap-stream bridge at Ban Nam Song, and was reported with a Highway 1256 (Pua–Bo Kluea) bridge collapse. Nation Thailand separately described flash floods and washed-out bridges in Pua, including a bridge in the Fai Chao weir area — a different named structure. No source fetched reported deaths at the Na Lao weir itself.
incidents.status: One side of the weir washed out; adjacent road damaged. Provincial heavy-rain warning in effect through at least 21 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: unknown
incidents.notes: Minor weir washout, not a reservoir-dam collapse. Fai Chao weir/bridge damage in Pua is a related flood impact, not merged into this record.
incidents.breach_size: one side of the weir washed away
incidents.investigating_agency: Nan provincial public relations office report

incidents.name: Kangimi Dam
incidents.location_label: Igabi LGA, Kaduna State, Nigeria
incidents.river_or_facility: Kangimi Dam
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: NSEMA warned of reported structural distress and visible cracks, with no breach reported as of 19 August 2026.
incidents.what_happened: The Niger State Emergency Management Agency issued an urgent public warning on Tuesday 18 August 2026 over reported structural distress and visible cracks at Kangimi Dam in Igabi LGA, Kaduna State. NSEMA Director-General Abdullahi Baba Arah said August rains raised the need for immediate technical assessment and that a major failure could flood downstream communities in Kaduna, Niger State, the FCT and adjoining areas. NSEMA asked the federal government, Kaduna State, dam operators, NEMA, the hydrological and meteorological agencies and security services to verify crack severity, map downstream risk and activate early warning and evacuation planning. Residents were told to stay calm, avoid waterways in heavy rain and ignore unverified rumours. No source fetched for this dataset reported a breach or uncontrolled release.
incidents.status: No breach reported as of 19 August 2026. Neighbouring-state emergency agency alert only; independent confirmation of crack severity by Kaduna/NEMA/dam operator not found in the articles fetched.
incidents.notes: This is a watch, not a failure. NSEMA is the downstream state's EMA, not the dam owner or Kaduna regulator.
incidents.downstream_risk: NSEMA said a major failure could flood communities in Kaduna, Niger State, the FCT and adjoining areas
incidents.investigating_agency: Niger State Emergency Management Agency (alert; not the dam owner)

incidents.name: Tarlac River flood-control dike (San Isidro, Zone 1)
incidents.region: Barangay San Isidro, Tarlac City, Tarlac

incidents.cause_summary: About 50 metres of a newly built flood-control dike collapsed as monsoon rain swelled the Tarlac River.
incidents.what_happened: Local outlet Tarlakenyo reported that about 50 metres of a newly built Tarlac River flood-control dike in Zone 1, Barangay San Isidro, collapsed around 04:00 on 17 August 2026 as monsoon rain swelled the river. The project, 'Repair / Rehabilitation / Improvement of Flood Control Structures along Tarlac River Control' under the 2025 GAA (about PHP 45.43 million, contractor GJE Builders Corporation), had been recorded 100% complete on 6 February 2026. DPWH Tarlac 1st District Engineering Office personnel assessed the damage while barangay officials, city and provincial governments, PNP and the Philippine Army sandbagged the new dike's end and part of an older dike. Vice Mayor KT Angeles said the contractor should restore the structure; Mayor Susan Yap warned residents to stay away because the collapse could widen or water could rise. No casualty figure appeared in the article fetched.
incidents.status: Partial dike collapse under emergency sandbagging and DPWH assessment as of 17 August 2026. Situation described as still volatile that day.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: unknown
incidents.notes: Single local-newsroom source plus on-the-record mayor/vice-mayor and DPWH presence. Prefer a national Philippine wire or DPWH release when one appears. Not a reservoir dam.

incidents.name: Lake Wynonah Dam
incidents.region: South Manheim Township, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania
incidents.location_label: South Manheim Township, Pennsylvania, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Plum Creek / Lake Wynonah (175-acre reservoir)
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: PADEP cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway and inability to pass a major flood.
incidents.what_happened: In a 14 August 2026 letter to the Lake Wynonah Property Owners Association, Kirk Kreider, acting chief of PADEP's Division of Dam Safety, declared the 1971 earthen Lake Wynonah Dam 'unsafe' and requested an immediate voluntary full drawdown of the 175-acre reservoir at up to one foot per day, with a formal order threatened if the association does not comply. The letter cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway, inability to pass a major flood, and temporary bracing of the top walls after a spillway collapse at the community's Fawn Lake Dam. Kreider wrote that 'unsafe' does not mean imminent failure, but that deficiencies could result in failure with loss of life or substantial property damage if not corrected. The lake had already been drawn down 10–15 feet in autumn 2025 after new seepage and a boil were reported. PADEP also said the high-hazard owner lacked required financial assurance.
incidents.status: PADEP unsafe designation and requested full drawdown in effect as of 17 August 2026 reporting; draft consent order/agreement with a four-week response window. Not an imminent-failure declaration.
incidents.notes: 2025 seepage drawdown is background. No 2026 breach. Fawn Lake Dam spillway collapse date was not independently sourced for this file.
incidents.downstream_risk: high-hazard dam; PADEP said failure could cause loss of life or substantial property damage if not corrected

incidents.name: Dikwena Chrome Tailings Storage Facility (Samancor)
incidents.location_label: Brits, North West, South Africa
incidents.river_or_facility: Dikwena Chrome mine TSF, Compartment 1B (unnamed tributary polluted)
incidents.cause_summary: The northern wall of Compartment 1B collapsed; the cause is not officially determined, and commentary about rainfall or over-deposition is not an official finding.
incidents.what_happened: The northern wall of Compartment 1B at Samancor Chrome's Dikwena tailings storage facility near Brits collapsed at about 17:30 on 13 August 2026, releasing almost all tailings/slimes stored in that compartment. The Department of Water and Sanitation said a railway embankment and berms at the adjacent Eland Mine stopped the slurry from reaching the R566 provincial road; mine infrastructure, a railway line and Eskom powerlines were damaged and an unnamed tributary was polluted. DWS, the Limpopo-Olifants Catchment Management Agency and the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources assessed the site; DWS issued a verbal directive stopping tailings deposition in any of the mine's TSFs pending investigation. Water samples were taken; laboratory results were still pending as of the 17 August government statement. EWN reported no fatalities or injuries; cleanup of access routes and power infrastructure was under way by 18 August.
incidents.status: Government investigation ongoing; tailings deposition halted; cleanup and water-quality testing in progress as of 18 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: No residential evacuation reported; sludge blocked Eland Mine (Maroelabult) access and cut power in Brits, Hennops and surrounding areas

incidents.notes: Cause not officially determined. Satellite/expert commentary in Daily Maverick discusses possible delayed rainfall infiltration and over-deposition; that is not an official finding.

incidents.name: Bowersock Dam
incidents.location_label: Lawrence, Kansas, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Kansas River (Kaw) / Bowersock Mills & Power Company
incidents.cause_summary: Owner said one of four inflatable rubber crest bladders was punctured by floating trees and debris and ripped from end to end; the concrete dam remained intact.
incidents.what_happened: The Lawrence Journal-World reported on 13 August 2026 that one of four inflatable rubber bladders on the crest of Bowersock Dam had been punctured by heavy floating debris and ripped from end to end. Co-owner Sarah Hill-Nelson said the No. 2 bladder failure left a gap that dropped the upstream millpond about six feet. The concrete dam was holding; there was no downstream flood wave. The city of Lawrence said the Kaw River Water Treatment Plant continued to operate, though low pond levels are less efficient for intake and filtration. The run-of-river dam supplies Kansas's only hydroelectric plant and maintains the pond for the city's water intake. Hill-Nelson said a replacement bladder would take about four months and cost upwards of $300,000, and that this was the first time a Lawrence bladder had been destroyed beyond repair (a 2021 seam tear had been stitched). Exact calendar day of the puncture was described only as recently before the Thursday 13 August article.
incidents.status: Concrete dam intact; No. 2 inflatable crest bladder destroyed; millpond about six feet below normal; water plant operating; repair approach undecided as of 13 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: No evacuation reported; KU rowing expected to be disrupted by low water
incidents.notes: Not a concrete-dam collapse. Incident date is the Journal-World report date; the owner said the puncture happened recently before that Thursday. Background dam dimensions (length ~655 ft, height ~17.08 ft, 423-acre impoundment) are from Wikipedia/LIHI, not from the 2026 incident article.
incidents.volume_released: millpond dropped about six feet; volume not stated
incidents.breach_size: No. 2 rubber crest bladder ripped end to end; concrete dam intact
incidents.downstream_risk: No downstream flooding reported; low water affects city intake efficiency and KU rowing
incidents.economic_damage: replacement bladder estimated upwards of $300,000 plus installation; full cost undecided

incidents.name: Beiru River and Jialu River levee breaches
incidents.region: Henan (Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan; Chuanhui District, Zhoukou)
incidents.location_label: Jiaxian County, Henan, China
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Changqiao Town, Jiaxian); Xinhua: Yuxi Village Beiru breach
incidents.river_or_facility: Beiru River; Jialu River (Shaying backwater)
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened levee breaches on the Beiru and Jialu rivers.
incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened a levee breach more than 40 metres wide on the Beiru River in Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan, on the night of Wednesday 12 August 2026; more than 2,000 people were relocated and Xinhua reported no casualties. That breach was sealed on Friday night 14 August after nearly two days of sandbagging, because heavy plant could not reach the narrow levee crown. A separate eastern-embankment breach on the Jialu River in Chuanhui District, Zhoukou, opened around 23:00 on Thursday 13 August, widening from about 30 metres to about 117 metres under Jialu inflows and Shaying River backwater. China Daily and People's Daily/Xinhua said the Jialu breach was sealed on Saturday night 15 August after more than 2,000 emergency personnel worked the site; crews continued raising, reinforcing and sealing seepage. A Level-IV national disaster-relief response was activated for Henan.
incidents.status: Both breaches reported sealed (Beiru 14 Aug; Jialu 15 Aug). Embankment raising, reinforcement and seepage control continuing at Jialu as of 15–16 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: More than 2,000 relocated from the Beiru breach; Jialu displacement not separately quantified in the English Xinhua/China Daily reports used
incidents.notes: Two distinct levee breaches grouped as one living-database item because they were the same Typhoon Dolphin flood episode. Zero deaths is the Beiru figure stated by Xinhua; no separate Jialu fatality figure was published in the reports fetched.
incidents.breach_size: Beiru more than 40 metres wide; Jialu widened from about 30 metres to about 117 metres
incidents.downstream_risk: more than 2,000 relocated from the Beiru breach

incidents.name: Olde Mill Golf Club Dam
incidents.location_label: Laurel Fork, Virginia, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Olde Mill Golf Resort lake / Stone Mountain Creek drainage toward Big Reed Island Creek
incidents.cause_summary: Intense rain was followed by failure of the primary spillway pipe; DCR said it had received none of the required owner documents since 2006 and the last emergency action plan expired in 2012.
incidents.what_happened: Intense rain on the night of 2 August 2026 flooded the Laurel Fork area of Carroll County. Virginia DCR Regional Engineer Steven Bricker observed on 4 August that the Olde Mill Golf Club lake (normal pool near 300 acre-feet) was almost completely drained after a partial breach. DCR's 5 August letter to owner Norris Mitchell / MG Golf Facilities LLC stated the primary spillway pipe failed, creating a scour hole around the riser and significant sediment loss; the dam has a preliminary high-hazard classification and may not impound water until corrective action. Downstream residents told Cardinal News at least 20 properties were damaged and estimated losses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars; they allege the dam intensified flooding. DCR said it had received none of the required owner documents since 2006 and the last emergency action plan expired in 2012. Owners were dewatering and beginning repairs as of mid-August; Carroll County said it issued no live alert because it learned of the flood after it ended.
incidents.status: Lake largely drained; DCR unsafe / non-imminent-danger notice in effect; dam not allowed to impound until corrective action; owner working on dewatering and spillway repair as of 18 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: At least 20 properties damaged (resident estimate reported by Cardinal News); no official evacuation figure
incidents.notes: Causal share of downstream flooding versus the rainstorm itself is disputed by residents and not adjudicated. NID inventory pages are background only and were not used for 2026 incident facts.
incidents.owner_operator: Norris Mitchell / MG Golf Facilities LLC
incidents.volume_released: lake almost completely drained after a partial breach
incidents.breach_size: primary spillway pipe failed, creating a scour hole around the riser
incidents.downstream_risk: Laurel Fork area; at least 20 properties damaged (resident estimate)
incidents.economic_damage: resident estimates in the hundreds of thousands of dollars

incidents.name: Chattamakhana Dam
incidents.location_label: Balangir district, Odisha, India
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Balangir district; ~18 km downstream of Lower Suktel)
incidents.river_or_facility: Chattamakhana Dam (about 18 km downstream of Lower Suktel Dam per the MLA letter)
incidents.cause_summary: The newly built dam suffered cut-off-wall and downstream-embankment damage in early-August rains; the MLA’s letter said the sanctioned design had reduced waterway, gates and impervious floor.
incidents.what_happened: Newly built Chattamakhana Dam in Balangir district suffered damage in rains in early August 2026. Balangir MLA Kalikesh Narayan Singh Deo wrote to Chief Minister (and water-resources minister) Mohan Charan Majhi saying the cut-off wall was washed away and downstream embankments failed, and asking for a time-bound independent technical inquiry with the State Dam Safety Organisation and outside experts. He said the EPC project's sanctioned design reduced waterway from 256 m to 206 m, gates from 18 to 14 and impervious floor from 80 m to 50 m, while design discharge stayed 2,760 cumec, and he questioned whether that flood had been reassessed after Lower Suktel Dam. New Indian Express and OrissaPOST published the letter on 8–9 August. No source fetched described a full dam collapse or casualties.
incidents.status: Embankment/cut-off damage reported; independent inquiry requested as of 9 August 2026. Not reported as a collapse. Government inquiry outcome not found in sources fetched.
incidents.notes: Facts on damage and design changes come from the MLA's written representation as reported by newspapers, not from a published government inspection report. Not a collapse.

incidents.name: Bagré Dam
incidents.region: Centre-Est / Bagré (downstream White Volta / northern Ghana on alert)
incidents.location_label: Bagré, Centre-Est, Burkina Faso
incidents.river_or_facility: Bagré Dam on the Nakambé / White Volta system
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: Ghana authorities monitored a possible controlled spill if rainfall pushed the reservoir to a stated threshold.
incidents.what_happened: Ghana's Water Resources Commission said on 4–5 August 2026 that SONABEL, operator of Burkina Faso's Bagré Dam, might begin a controlled spill from 11 August if the reservoir reached a critical level (WRC cited 232.93 m / 62.77% full on 4 August). NADMO later said SONABEL deferred the 11 August spill because upstream rainfall was lower than expected; as of that day the level was 233.08 m, 1.92 m below a 234.15 m threshold cited by NADMO. A Citi Newsroom report of SONABEL's 15 August update put Bagré at 233.24 m (77.35% full), 1.76 m below the 235 m normal reservoir level, and said SONABEL may open spillway gates if the level reaches 234.75 m, with public notice before any release. This is a seasonal controlled-spill watch, not a structural failure. Northern Ghana communities along the White Volta remained on alert.
incidents.status: No spill started as of the 15 August 2026 SONABEL figures reported by Citi Newsroom. Reservoir below stated spill thresholds; Ghana NADMO/WRC still monitoring.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: NADMO placed White Volta basin communities on alert (68 communities cited in Northern Region coverage); no flood from a 2026 Bagré spill reported in sources fetched
incidents.notes: Not a dam failure. Spill-threshold figures differ slightly across WRC, NADMO and the 15 August SONABEL update; all agree the dam had not spilled as of those reports.

incidents.downstream_risk: White Volta basin communities on alert (68 communities cited in Northern Region coverage); no 2026 spill reported

incidents.name: Ngawun River embankment (Laymyethna)
incidents.location_label: Laymyethna, Ayeyarwady Region, Myanmar

incidents.what_happened: Heavy monsoon rain and riverbank erosion breached the Ngawun River embankment in Laymyethna Township on the night of 30 July 2026. Eleven Media, citing the President's Office Information and Public Relations Bureau, said that by 5 August floodwater had entered five Laymyethna wards, major town roads and 106 villages across four townships, with more than 30,000 people affected in Laymyethna Township alone. AHA Centre Flash Update No. 1 of 19 August, citing DDM Myanmar as of 18 August 16:30 UTC+7, reported flooding of five urban wards, major roads and 150 surrounding villages, with 63,000 people affected and 15,000 displaced households in Ayeyarwady (Laymyethna, Hinthada, Yekyi, Kyangin), plus 1 death in that regional tally. DDM and partners were still repairing breached embankment sections with geo-bags, sandbags and other works; the government had provided about USD 85,200 in assistance. Heavy rain was forecast to persist through 23 August.
incidents.status: Breach repair and flood control still under way as of the 19 August 2026 AHA update; further heavy rain warned.

incidents.name: Swift Creek Upper Reservoir
incidents.region: Afton / Swift Creek Canyon, Lincoln County, Wyoming
incidents.location_label: Afton, Wyoming, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Swift Creek Upper Reservoir (Lower Valley Energy hydro)
incidents.cause_summary: The sluice gate failed, causing an uncontrolled release; a camera inspection found catastrophic gate failure, destroyed panels and a broken operating rod.
incidents.what_happened: Lower Valley Energy said the sluice gate at Swift Creek Upper Reservoir failed in the early morning of 13 July 2026, causing an uncontrolled release that substantially drained the reservoir and carried sediment, trees and debris downstream (including material from a 2023 upstream landslide). Town of Afton staff told SVI the town water supply was not affected. CEO Bear Prairie later said a camera inspection found catastrophic gate failure, destroyed panels, and a broken operating rod; debris then partly plugged the opening and flows stabilised at a low reservoir level. LVE said the dam itself remains safe and is monitored. Permanent gate replacement requires FERC, U.S. Forest Service and other approvals, with at least a 60-day FERC review after the repair plan is submitted. The public was told to stay out of the reservoir bed and canyon.
incidents.status: Reservoir largely drained and held at a low level; dam reported safe and monitored; sluice-gate replacement plan in regulatory review as of late-July 2026 LVE/SVI updates. No deaths reported.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: No evacuation reported; public exclusion of reservoir and Swift Creek canyon

incidents.what_happened: Typhoon Maysak rain caused Liulan Reservoir in Hengzhou to overtop and breach on 6 July 2026. Nanning raised flood-control emergency response to Level I; CCTV video showed a large release through the dam breach. At a 9 July news conference, Nanning Vice-Mayor Ding Wei said the Liulan breach had caused 26 deaths (5 then unidentified) and 7 people missing, while Guangxi overall had 39 dead and 9 missing — figures that could overlap pending DNA identification. Deputy water-resources director Zhai Jianjia said Liulan water had fallen below dam-foundation rock, the breach and discharge had largely stabilised, and crest access was restored that morning for dredging. Nanning reported 64,500 people evacuated or resettled by 11:00 on 9 July (54,500 in Hengzhou; 9,321 in Binyang).
incidents.status: Breach and downstream discharge reported largely stable as of 9 July 2026; search, identification, resettlement and a later State Council investigation were reported in subsequent Chinese coverage.

incidents.name: Dudhkumar river protection dyke (Muriarhat)
incidents.location_label: Nageshwari, Kurigram, Bangladesh
incidents.river_or_facility: Dudhkumar River protection dyke, Muriarhat / Adarshapara
incidents.cause_summary: Nearly 40 metres of river-protection dyke collapsed as the Dudhkumar ran 22 cm above its danger level, and floodwater entered villages through the gap.
incidents.what_happened: The Daily Star of 30 June 2026 reported that nearly 40 metres of Dudhkumar river-protection dyke collapsed late the previous night (29 June; a farmer quoted the paper said Monday night) at Muriarhat in Bamandanga union, Nageshwari, Kurigram, as the river ran 22 cm above its 29.60 m danger level at Pateshwari. BWDB executive engineer Rakibul Hasan said floodwater entered villages through the gap; the Bamandanga Union Parishad chairman said at least eight villages and about 5,000 families were stranded. A farmer said water entered around 250 households. BWDB prepared bamboo piling and sand-filled geobags. A 5 July Daily Star follow-up said water was receding and BWDB had started placing geobags on an unfinished 300-metre stretch of a 3,100-metre right-bank embankment delayed by land acquisition. No death toll for the dyke breach was given in those articles.

incidents.name: Sardoba Reservoir dam

incidents.river_or_facility: Sardoba Reservoir on the Southern Mirzachul / Hungry Steppe canal system
incidents.cause_summary: A recently completed earth embankment breached at picket 6 after days of stormy weather. Later InSAR work points to differential settlement and internal erosion rather than rainfall overtopping.
incidents.what_happened: At 05:55 on 1 May 2020 water began overflowing the 6th picket wall of Uzbekistan's Sardoba Reservoir, completed only in 2017 to store about 922 million cubic metres for irrigation in Sirdaryo and Jizzakh. Uzbekistan's Ministry of Emergency Situations said 11,598 people were moved the first day and about 60,450 the next; later tallies put evacuations above 70,000 in Uzbekistan plus more than 5,000 in Kazakhstan. incidents.cause_summary: A sinkhole opened under a phosphogypsum stack, tearing the liner and draining contaminated process water into the Floridan Aquifer.
incidents.what_happened: On 27 August 2016 Mosaic monitoring showed about a 2-foot drop in a gypsum-stack pond at the New Wales phosphate plant south of Mulberry, Florida. Reuters and the Lakeland Ledger reported that a sinkhole later confirmed about 45 feet wide damaged the liner and drained the pond into the Floridan Aquifer. The Ledger, citing Mosaic, said about 215 million gallons of contaminated water entered the aquifer; WISE cites 840,000 m³ as of 17 September 2016 (similar order of magnitude). Florida DEP was notified 28 August and oversaw recovery wells. Mosaic said monitoring had not shown off-site contamination a mile away. No deaths.
incidents.status: Sinkhole remediated under DEP/EPA oversight; plant operations continued.
incidents.notes: Containment failure via sinkhole, not a classic embankment collapse. 215 million gallons ≈ 814,000 m³, close to WISE's 840,000 m³.

incidents.name: Gilgel Gibe II headrace tunnel
incidents.region: Oromia Region, about 80 km east of Jimma

incidents.cause_summary: About 15 m of the new 26 km headrace tunnel caved in days after inauguration; contractor called it an unforeseen geological event in the Rift Valley.
incidents.what_happened: Ethiopia inaugurated the 420 MW Gilgel Gibe II station on 14 January 2010. Wikipedia and contemporary reports (VOA, ENR, International Rivers, Tunnel Talk) say that about ten days later roughly 15 m of the 26 km concrete-lined headrace under Fofa Mountain collapsed, shutting the plant. Salini Costruttori blamed an unforeseen geological cave-in; critics pointed to rushed construction, a no-bid contract and known Rift Valley faults. The rest of the tunnel was described as intact. Repairs finished and generation resumed on 26 December 2010. No deaths are recorded in the sources fetched.

incidents.name: West Quincy / Fabius River Drainage District levee
incidents.region: Marion County, Missouri (West Quincy, opposite Quincy, Illinois)
incidents.location_label: West Quincy levee at the Bayview Bridge approach, Missouri
incidents.geo_source: West Quincy / US 24 Bayview Bridge Missouri approach
incidents.river_or_facility: Fabius River Levee and Drainage District (West Quincy stem)
incidents.cause_summary: During the 1993 Mississippi flood the West Quincy levee opened on 16 July, flooding about 14,000 acres and closing the last highway bridge for ~200 miles. A later criminal conviction for sabotage remains contested by soil-science testimony.
incidents.what_happened: On the night of 16 July 1993 the heavily sandbagged West Quincy levee on the Missouri bank of the Mississippi failed about 20:20. Floodwater closed the Bayview Bridge — then the only open highway span for roughly 200 miles — wrecked a truck-body plant, a rail yard and more than 20 small businesses, and inundated about 14,000 acres. A barge was pulled through the gap and a gas station exploded. James Scott was later convicted of causing a catastrophe; defense experts argued natural seepage or last-minute bulldozer work on the levee. The record treats the event as a named 1993 flood levee failure; the criminal finding is noted, not adopted as the engineering cause.

incidents.what_happened: Portuguese Wikipedia and a USU cascade-failure paper describe the 19–20 January 1977 Rio Pardo disaster. After three weeks of rain and about 180 mm in 24 hours, CESP operators did not open Euclides da Cunha's floodgates in time (Gazeta do Rio Pardo later quoted a witness that an earlier operator had been sacked for opening gates without São Paulo's leave). Overtopping began about 20:30 on 19 January; the 56 m earth dam breached about 03:30 on the 20th, some 100 m from the right abutment, releasing more than 13 million m³. About 30 minutes later the 35 m Limoeiro / Salles de Oliveira dam 10 km downstream also failed, adding about 25 million m³. Folha de S.Paulo's 21 January 1977 front page said the river broke four dams and flooded nine towns. Both plants were rebuilt; Euclides da Cunha now has 108.8 MW.

incidents.cause_summary: The 1973 Mississippi flood undermined the low-sill structure; a wing wall failed and emergency rock was dumped to keep the river from jumping into the Atchafalaya.
incidents.what_happened: USACE's Old River Control Complex, completed in 1963, is meant to keep about 70 percent of combined Mississippi–Red flow in the main river and 30 percent in the Atchafalaya. In the 1973 flood the low-sill structure was loaded far above design. Scour and piping under the stilling basin and a wing-wall failure put the structure at risk of losing the river. Barges of rock were sunk and dumped to armor the foundation. The river did not avulse. USACE later added the Auxiliary Structure (1986) so the low sill would never again take the whole load. No deaths at the structure. This is a named near-loss of the lower Mississippi alignment, not a reservoir-dam collapse.

incidents.cause_summary: A coal-refuse impoundment failed after rain; state and federal inquiries found improper construction, while the company called it an act of God.
incidents.what_happened: A Pittston Coal coal-refuse impoundment failed about 08:00 on 26 February 1972 after rain, releasing about 132 million gallons of water and slurry. The flood overwhelmed two downstream refuse dams and destroyed or damaged 16–17 coal-camp communities along Buffalo Creek Hollow. State and federal inquiries found improper construction; the company called it an act of God. The disaster drove federal coal-refuse impoundment regulation.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 4,000 of 5,000 valley residents left homeless

incidents.name: Certej tailings dam
incidents.location_label: Certej gold-mine tailings pond, Hunedoara County, Romania
incidents.river_or_facility: Certej tailings dam
incidents.cause_summary: A 16-expert government commission found the pond had been raised above allowed height and contained heterogeneous deposits (1936-1971) that created a slip plane.
incidents.what_happened: At 04:55 on 30 October 1971 an 80 m breach opened in the Certej cyanide-tailings dam. About 300,000 m3 of residue flooded a 4-5 km radius, destroying six apartment blocks, a dormitory and seven houses. Eighty-nine people died and 76 were injured, most still asleep. Communist authorities announced only 48 deaths to avoid a national day of mourning. Prosecutors later dropped charges.
incidents.status: historical / town rebuilt; mine later redeveloped as a separate project
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Certej apartment district destroyed; survivors rehoused by the state
incidents.notes: Investigation figure 89 dead / 76 injured. Official press at the time said 48. Pond used 1936-1971.

incidents.name: Lower San Fernando Dam (Van Norman)
incidents.location_label: Lower Van Norman Reservoir, Los Angeles, California, United States
incidents.geo_source: Van Norman / Lower San Fernando Dam site, northern San Fernando Valley (USGS / ASDSO case-study location)
incidents.river_or_facility: Lower San Fernando Dam (Van Norman)
incidents.cause_summary: The Mw 6.6 San Fernando earthquake liquefied hydraulic sand fill in the upstream shell. A major slide dropped the crest until only a thin remnant retained the reservoir.
incidents.what_happened: On 9 February 1971 the San Fernando (Sylmar) earthquake caused a large upstream slide at Lower San Fernando Dam about 40 seconds after strong shaking. The 142-ft hydraulic-fill dam lost about 30 ft of crest. About 80,000 people in an 11-square-mile area downstream were evacuated for four days while pumps lowered about 10,000 acre-feet. No dam-failure deaths. The dam was replaced by Los Angeles Dam. The wider earthquake killed about 65 people (not attributed to this dam).
incidents.status: replaced by Los Angeles Dam; original structure taken out of service
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 80,000 evacuated for four days

sources.label: USGS Fact Sheet 096-95 — The Los Angeles Dam Story

incidents.notes: Near-failure / incident, not a completed breach. deaths=0 refers to the dam event; do not assign the earthquake's ~65 regional deaths. Cause tailings_liquefaction used for hydraulic-fill liquefaction (vocabulary has no separate hydraulic_fill term).
incidents.owner_operator: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
incidents.investigating_agency: Seed et al. and subsequent seismic dam-safety investigations

incidents.name: Mufulira No. 3 tailings dam (underground inrush)
incidents.location_label: Mufulira copper mine, Copperbelt, Zambia
incidents.geo_source: Mufulira town centroid (mine adjoins the town); exact No. 3 pond not independently surveyed
incidents.river_or_facility: Mufulira No. 3 tailings dam (underground inrush)
incidents.cause_summary: A sinkhole opened under the No. 3 slimes dam after years of cave mining beneath the impoundment, dumping water and tailings into underground workings. Prior sinkholes and minor mud ingress had been inadequately investigated.
incidents.what_happened: At about 02:55 on 25 September 1970 roughly 450,000 m3 to 2 million tonnes of water and slimes from Mufulira's No. 3 tailings dam rushed into the Peterson section of the underground copper mine. Within about 15 minutes eastern workings were overwhelmed. Of about 1,500 men on shift, 89 were killed (64 mine employees and 25 Cementation Ltd contractors). It remains Zambia's worst mine disaster.
incidents.status: historical / mine later rehabilitated with changed tailings and cave-mining practice
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 1,500 miners on shift; widows and orphans later resettled

incidents.volume_released: about 450,000 m3 of sludge into the mine (Tembo); about 1 million tonnes also cited
incidents.investigating_agency: mine and Zambian official inquiries after the disaster

incidents.name: Dique Frías (Mendoza)
incidents.region: Piedmont west of Mendoza city, Mendoza Province
incidents.location_label: Dique Frías on Arroyo Frías, Mendoza, Argentina
incidents.river_or_facility: Dique Frías (Mendoza flood-control dam) on Arroyo Frías
incidents.cause_summary: A 15 m rockfill flood-control dam was overwhelmed by a 105 mm/hour cloudburst; the basin was undersized and outlets did not pass the debris-laden flood.
incidents.what_happened: On 4 January 1970 a piedmont storm (about 105 mm in one hour) destroyed the Frías torrent dam west of Mendoza. Capitanelli's 1970 UNCuyo report, written for the provincial inquiry, called it the city's worst disaster since the 1861 earthquake and said the 140,000 m³ basin was too small — as an 1939 flood had already shown. Water forced the intake tower and spillway; the dam overtopped and collapsed. Secondary sources give 24–100 deaths (commonly 24–42) and 1,500–2,000 people affected, with more than 1,000 cars destroyed and US$20–23 million damage. The flood ran down the Frías zanjón into the city.
incidents.status: Destroyed; Mendoza later rebuilt a stepped torrent-control system.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 1,500–2,000 people affected (secondary compilations)

sources.label: Capitanelli 1970 — Causas de la destrucción del Dique Frías (UNCuyo)
zxc.wiki — Frías dam (coordinates and casualty range)

incidents.notes: Deaths left null because published figures range from 24 to 100 and the 1970 inquiry text fetched does not give an official count.
incidents.breach_size: dam destroyed
incidents.downstream_risk: western Mendoza city / zanjón Frías

Emergency drawdown followed; the emergency phase ended in May 1970. The near-breach, with Warmwithens 1970, was a factor in the Reservoirs Act 1975. No deaths.

incidents.name: Lake Lee Dam (Mud Pond rebuild)
incidents.location_label: Lake Lee / Mud Pond / Basin Pond on Greenwater Brook, East Lee, Berkshire County, Massachusetts
incidents.geo_source: named East Lee / Basin Pond area centroid; same site as 1886 Mud Pond Dam
incidents.river_or_facility: Lake Lee Dam (Mud Pond rebuild), Greenwater Brook
incidents.cause_summary: Tighe and Bond investigation (November 1968) cited numerous irregularities; the dam did not conform to the submitted architectural plans. Failed after heavy March rain, about 2.5-3 years after construction on the 1886 footprint.
incidents.what_happened: The about 25-foot earthen Lake Lee dam, built 1965 for a leisure-home development on the old Mud Pond site, collapsed on 24 March 1968. About 12 million gallons went down Greenwater Brook. Edward Gage, 61, and Olive Cordonier were killed on Cape Street. The Massachusetts Turnpike embankment acted as a partial dike. The disaster led to the 1970 Mud Pond Bill giving the state dam-inspection authority.
incidents.status: not rebuilt as a development dam; site is now Basin Pond

incidents.name: Wolf Creek Dam (karst foundation seepage)
incidents.location_label: Wolf Creek Dam on the Cumberland River, Lake Cumberland, Kentucky
incidents.geo_source: named Wolf Creek Dam / Jamestown–Russell Springs area, Kentucky
incidents.river_or_facility: Wolf Creek Dam, Cumberland River / Lake Cumberland
incidents.cause_summary: Karst limestone foundation developed solution channels and piping. Sinkholes and muddy outflow appeared at the downstream toe in 1967-68. Emergency grouting 1968-70 is credited with saving the dam.
incidents.what_happened: Wolf Creek Dam (completed 1951-52; 258 feet high, 5,736 feet long) showed muddy tailrace flow in late 1967. On 13 March 1968 a sinkhole opened near the downstream toe in the wraparound embankment (one account: about 40 feet deep). A third sinkhole opened 22 April 1968. Emergency grouting 1968-70, a concrete cutoff wall 1975-79, reservoir restriction from 2005, and a later deeper barrier wall addressed continuing seepage. The dam did not breach.
incidents.status: remediated with cutoff/barrier walls; still in service (USACE)

sources.label: Missouri S&T thesis — Wolf Creek Dam foundation remediation

incidents.notes: Serious seepage / near-failure incident, not a breach. Cited pages do not state fatalities. Deaths left null. Incident date is the 13 March 1968 sinkhole that made the emergency public.
incidents.reservoir_capacity: about 6 million acre-feet (Lake Cumberland; master's thesis)
incidents.investigating_agency: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; DSAC peer review (2006)

incidents.name: Iwiny / Konrad copper-mine tailings dam
incidents.location_label: Iwiny, near Konrad copper mine, Poland

incidents.what_happened: About 03:00-03:15 on 13 December 1967 the tailings-pond dike at Konrad copper mine near Iwiny breached. A roughly 6 m wave of water and flotation waste flooded Iwiny and neighbouring villages. Eighteen people died, about 570 were injured or otherwise harmed, and about 150 buildings were damaged or destroyed.
incidents.status: historical / dam rebuilt with state funds; mine area later closed
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Iwiny and neighbouring villages; about 150 buildings

incidents.name: Sempor Dam
incidents.location_label: Sempor River, Gombong, Kebumen, Central Java, Indonesia

incidents.what_happened: On 29 November 1967 flash floods overtopped Sempor Dam on the Sempor River during its first construction season (begun 1967). incidents.name: Fontenelle Dam
incidents.location_label: Green River, Fontenelle Dam, Wyoming, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Fontenelle Dam
incidents.cause_summary: During first filling, unprotected relief joints in the foundation cutoff allowed reservoir water to erode embankment soils (hydraulic piping) at the right/west abutment. Emergency rockfill and rapid drawdown prevented a full breach.
incidents.what_happened: On 3 September 1965 a leak at Fontenelle Dam's west abutment grew into a large downstream cavity (on the order of 80 ft wide, 50-60 ft deep, 170-200 ft long). About 10,000 cubic yards of embankment slid into the stilling basin. On 6 September a 15-by-20 ft sinkhole 30 ft deep opened on the crest, leaving only about 45 ft of dam between the hole and the downstream face. USBR dumped riprap and lowered the 345,000 acre-foot reservoir about 4 ft/day. Emergency releases flooded ranches and homes along the Green River. No deaths.

incidents.name: Lower Hell Hole Dam (construction failure)
incidents.location_label: Rubicon River, Hell Hole, Sierra Nevada, California, United States
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Hell Hole Reservoir 39.08011N 120.39230W (1966 replacement dam; 1964 failure was the partially built dam at this site)
incidents.river_or_facility: Lower Hell Hole Dam (construction failure)
incidents.cause_summary: A partially completed zoned rockfill (downstream shell about 220 ft, impervious core only tens of feet) was overtopped through the porous rockfill after about 22 inches of rain in five days and a blocked diversion outlet.
incidents.what_happened: On 23 December 1964 the incomplete Lower Hell Hole Dam on the Rubicon River collapsed. About 30,000 acre-feet of water and 700,000 cubic yards of rock surged about 60 miles down the Rubicon/American River, destroying two suspension bridges and the Highway 49 bridge near Auburn before Folsom Lake absorbed the flood. No deaths. A replacement dam was completed in 1966.
incidents.status: replaced 1966; present Lower Hell Hole Dam operating (Placer County Water Agency)
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: remote canyon; five bridges destroyed including Highway 49 at Auburn

incidents.name: Swift and Two Medicine Dams (Blackfeet Flood)
incidents.location_label: Blackfeet Indian Reservation, Montana, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Birch Creek / Two Medicine Creek
incidents.cause_summary: A rain-on-snow storm produced extreme runoff; Swift Dam failed and additional Reservation deaths were attributed to extreme spillway discharge at Lower Two Medicine Dam.
incidents.what_happened: A rain-on-snow storm in early June 1964 produced extreme runoff across northwestern Montana. Swift Dam failed about 10:10 on 8 June, killing 19 people on the Blackfeet Reservation. Lower Two Medicine Dam also failed; nine additional Reservation deaths were attributed to extreme spillway discharge before that failure. USGS documented the flood; Gibson Dam overtopped but held.
incidents.status: historical / both failed dams later addressed; statewide flood remains a USGS reference storm
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 8,700 evacuated statewide during the high-water period
incidents.notes: Deaths: 19 from Swift failure + 9 associated with Two Medicine spillway flooding (USGS/ASDSO). Statewide flood deaths were 30.
incidents.owner_operator: Pondera Canal and Reservoir Company (Swift); Bureau of Indian Affairs (Two Medicine)
incidents.downstream_risk: Blackfeet Reservation communities along Birch Creek and Two Medicine Creek
incidents.economic_damage: statewide flood damages over $500 million in 2020 dollars

incidents.name: Baldwin Hills Dam
incidents.location_label: Los Angeles, California, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Baldwin Hills Reservoir (LADWP)
incidents.cause_summary: Investigations linked the breach to foundation displacement along the Newport–Inglewood fault system, with oil-field operations later the subject of civil settlement.
incidents.what_happened: A caretaker noticed lining leakage on the morning of 14 December 1963; police evacuated about 1,600 people before the Baldwin Hills Reservoir dam breached at 15:38. About 250–290 million gallons flooded a square mile of South Los Angeles, destroying or damaging 277 homes. Investigations linked the breach to foundation displacement along the Newport–Inglewood fault system, with oil-field operations later the subject of civil settlement.
incidents.status: historical / reservoir not rebuilt; site is now Kenneth Hahn State Recreation Area
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 1,600 evacuated; 277 homes destroyed or damaged
incidents.notes: Five named fatalities. Early detection and evacuation are credited with preventing a far larger death toll.
incidents.owner_operator: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
incidents.downstream_risk: South Los Angeles neighbourhoods; about 1,600 evacuated; 277 homes destroyed or damaged
incidents.investigating_agency: civil engineering investigations of the Baldwin Hills Reservoir failure

incidents.name: Vajont Dam landslide and overtopping
incidents.location_label: Longarone / Erto e Casso, Veneto–Friuli, Italy
incidents.river_or_facility: Vajont / Piave (Longarone)
incidents.cause_summary: During first filling a landslide from Monte Toc entered the reservoir and generated a wave that overtopped the intact dam wall, destroying Longarone and nearby villages.
incidents.what_happened: During first filling, a roughly 260-million-cubic-metre landslide from Monte Toc entered the Vajont reservoir at 22:39, generating a wave that overtopped the dam by about 250 m. About 50 million cubic metres of water destroyed Longarone and nearby villages in minutes. The concrete arch dam itself remained essentially intact. Official data speak of 1,917 victims; higher estimates exist because many bodies were never identified.

incidents.what_happened: The 75-foot zoned earthfill irrigation dam, built 1961-62 for the South Kamas-Washington Irrigation Company, failed on the morning of 16 June 1963 during first filling (about 1,200 acre-feet stored). incidents.name: Spaulding Pond Dam (Mohegan Park)
incidents.location_label: Mohegan Park, Norwich, Connecticut, United States
incidents.geo_source: USGS/TopoQuest Spaulding Pond Dam Number 1 N41.54649 W72.07008 (pond site of the 1963 embankment)
incidents.river_or_facility: Spaulding Pond Dam (Mohegan Park)
incidents.cause_summary: A century-old earthen dam with a history of seepage leaked during two days of rain, then failed at night. Local official reports described a growing hole in the embankment.
incidents.what_happened: On the evening of 6 March 1963 the earthen Spaulding Pond Dam in Mohegan Park, Norwich, failed after rain and after seepage had been inspected that afternoon and judged not immediately dangerous. At about 21:27 the dam collapsed. A wall of water and thick ice slabs hit downtown Norwich. Five workers died when Turner-Stanton Mill collapsed; Margaret Moody was killed while evacuating. Damage was more than $6 million.
incidents.status: historical / dam later rebuilt (mid-1960s NRCS structure at the pond)

incidents.investigating_agency: City of Norwich corporation counsel report (18 March 1963)

incidents.name: Panshet and Khadakwasla Dams
incidents.location_label: Pune, Maharashtra, India
incidents.river_or_facility: Ambi / Mutha River
incidents.cause_summary: Unfinished Panshet failed after outlet-conduit problems and first-filling stresses; the flood then overtopped and breached older masonry Khadakwasla downstream.
incidents.what_happened: The unfinished earthen Panshet Dam failed in the early hours of 12 July 1961 after outlet-conduit problems and first-filling stresses. The flood wave then overtopped and breached the older masonry Khadakwasla Dam downstream. Central Pune was inundated; Khadakwasla’s temporary resistance after dawn allowed many residents to move to higher ground. The event remains the city’s defining flood disaster.
incidents.status: historical / both dams later rebuilt; Pune floodplain planning still references 1961
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: tens of thousands homeless; over 100,000 homes reported damaged in later summaries

incidents.name: Kurenivka clay-slurry dam (Babi Yar / brick-factory impoundment)
incidents.location_label: Babi Yar clay-pulp dump above Kurenivka, Kyiv, Ukraine
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Kurenivka mudslide / Babi Yar 50°26′40″N 30°32′44″E (dam was at the edge of this ravine)
incidents.river_or_facility: Kurenivka clay-slurry dam (Babi Yar / brick-factory impoundment)
incidents.cause_summary: A dam holding loam pulp from a brick factory above Babi Yar collapsed after rain. Wikipedia and later Ukrainian documentary work cite design flaws and poor maintenance.
incidents.what_happened: At 09:20 on 13 March 1961 a dam securing a brick-factory loam-pulp dump at the edge of Babi Yar failed. Up to 600,000 m3 of pulp, mud, water and human remains from the ravine flowed down into Kurenivka, hitting a tram depot, industry, a cemetery and streets, in places 4 m deep. Soviet official deaths were 145; a 2012 Institute of Ukrainian History volume and later investigations estimate closer to 1,500. Authorities forbade memorials and dispersed burials.
incidents.status: historical / site later landscaped; memorial exists
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Kurenivka neighbourhood, tram depot and nearby industry inundated

sources.label: RFE/RL — The Deadly Mudslide The KGB Tried To Cover Up

incidents.location_label: La Luciana TSF, Reocín zinc-lead mine, Besaya valley, Cantabria, Spain

incidents.cause_summary: Seepage-induced flow failure of an upstream-raised Pb-Zn tailings dam. A 2025 forensic paper documents contractive layers, a high phreatic surface and a decant pond too close to the crest.
incidents.what_happened: At about 22:40 on 17 August 1960 the La Luciana tailings dam of Real Compañía Asturiana de Minas / AZSA at Reocín failed. WISE records about 100,000 m3 released and 18 dead; a 2025 Minerals forensic paper cites about 300,000 m3, 18 fatalities, farmland and lakes buried, and contamination of the Besaya. Two lakes disappeared and more than 11 ha were submerged. The breach scar remains; the facility was never properly closed.

incidents.name: Açude Orós (Presidente Juscelino Kubitschek de Oliveira)
incidents.location_label: Jaguaribe River at Orós, Ceará, Brazil
incidents.river_or_facility: Açude Orós on the Rio Jaguaribe
incidents.cause_summary: Partial collapse of the unfinished earth dam after torrential rain; DNOCS records water overtopping the wall under construction at 00:17 on 26 March 1960.
incidents.what_happened: At 00:17 on 26 March 1960, while the Orós dam on the Jaguaribe was still under construction, torrential rain caused a partial failure of the right abutment (DNOCS; O Povo). DNOCS says water first overtopped the wall, washed the fill, and then destroyed part of the dam. O Povo (2025 anniversary) says the right abutment gave way and reported 3.5 billion cubic metres released down the Jaguaribe, flooding Limoeiro do Norte, Jaguaribara, Jaguaribe and Aracati. DNOCS, citing Banco do Nordeste, says 170,000 people were directly affected (about 60% of the lower Jaguaribe population then). Portuguese Wikipedia states about 1,000 victims; O Povo and DNOCS say there are no official fatality records. President Juscelino Kubitschek ordered reconstruction; the dam was inaugurated 11 January 1961. Wikipedia PT gives completed reservoir capacity 2.1 billion m³.
incidents.status: Rebuilt and in service as Ceará's second-largest reservoir after Castanhão.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 170,000 people directly affected (Banco do Nordeste via DNOCS)

Courts did not assign criminal liability to the builders.

incidents.name: Hebgen Dam (earthquake seiche overtopping)
incidents.location_label: Madison River at Hebgen Lake, southwest Montana (near West Yellowstone)
incidents.river_or_facility: Hebgen Dam, Madison River / Hebgen Lake
incidents.cause_summary: The 17 August 1959 Mw 7.3 Hebgen Lake earthquake generated seiches that overtopped the dam four times (ASDSO: 3-4 feet deep, 5-10 minutes). The concrete-core embankment cracked but did not collapse.
incidents.what_happened: Just before midnight on 17 August 1959 a magnitude about 7.3 earthquake struck near Hebgen Lake. Seiches overtopped Hebgen Dam four times. The 85-foot concrete-core earthen dam was damaged (core-wall cracking, spillway damage, some downstream-slope erosion) but held. Downstream, a 36-43 million cubic yard rockslide dammed the Madison River and formed Quake Lake. The dam was repaired weeks later.

incidents.location_label: Heiwa Reservoir on a Toshitani River tributary, Kameoka

incidents.location_label: Wister Lake Dam on the Poteau River, Wister, Oklahoma

incidents.cause_summary: Near-failure by piping through the embankment in 1949. Differential settlement cracked the rolled earthfill; dispersive clay and lack of a sand filter allowed internal erosion. Emergency repairs in 1949-50 later judged to have hydrofractured the embankment.
incidents.what_happened: Wister Dam (rolled earthfill, 5,700 feet long, 99 feet high) was completed, and conservation-pool filling begun, in 1949. A downstream sand filter and an upstream plastic-concrete slurry wall were built (major rehabilitation completed 1990).

incidents.name: Columbia River railroad-fill levee (Vanport)
incidents.location_label: Spokane, Portland and Seattle Railway berm / west levee at Vanport, between Portland and the Columbia River
incidents.river_or_facility: Columbia River / Smith Lake west levee at Vanport
incidents.cause_summary: A 1907 railroad fill used as the west dike was not designed as a flood levee. It failed from the inside under hydrostatic load (Oregonian: high freeboard prevented overtopping). ASDSO: internal erosion under extreme Columbia flood.
incidents.what_happened: At about 16:17 on Memorial Day 30 May 1948 a roughly 200-foot section of the SP&S railroad berm holding back the Columbia River collapsed. A wall of water about 10 feet high entered Vanport. The wartime housing city (about 18,500 people) was underwater by nightfall and was never rebuilt. incidents.status: historical / remnants of dam and spillway remain; not rebuilt as a storage project

incidents.name: Schaeffer Dam (Lake McNeil / Beaver Creek Dam)
incidents.location_label: Beaver Creek above Penrose, Fremont County, Colorado, United States
incidents.geo_source: Penrose, Colorado town centroid; dam stood on Beaver Creek west of Penrose (ASDSO case study). Exact ruins not independently surveyed.
incidents.river_or_facility: Schaeffer Dam (Lake McNeil / Beaver Creek Dam)
incidents.cause_summary: A June 1921 cloudburst sequence, later classed by USGS as an extreme (order of 10,000-year) storm on Beaver Creek, overtopped the hydraulic-fill earth dam after the 100-ft spillway was overwhelmed. Uneven crest settlement concentrated overtopping in the middle 75 ft.
incidents.what_happened: After two days of Arkansas Valley cloudbursts, Schaeffer Dam on Beaver Creek overtopped on the morning of 5 June 1921 and failed, emptying about 3,600 acre-feet in roughly 30 minutes. USGS estimated a 153,000 cfs breach wave. The 3-5 June Pueblo flood killed an estimated 150-250 people (not assigned to this dam). Because the breach came after the main Arkansas crest, communities were already on high ground and ASDSO/USGS report no lives lost to the dam break. The dam was not rebuilt.
incidents.status: historical / not rebuilt; ruins and control tower remain (private land / BLM Schaeffer Dam Loop)
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Penrose fruit district; 10 miles of Beaver Creek and 11 miles of the Arkansas stripped of topsoil

incidents.breach_size: about 500 ft top width, 300 ft bottom width

incidents.name: Fullerton Dam (Turkey Creek irrigation dam)
incidents.location_label: Turkey Creek, 7 miles NW of Olustee, Jackson County, Oklahoma
incidents.river_or_facility: Fullerton Dam on Turkey Creek
incidents.cause_summary: A 1890s limestone-and-earth irrigation dam on Turkey Creek broke for good in a 1919 flood and was abandoned.
incidents.what_happened: Farmer William J. Fullerton built a gravity-flow irrigation dam of quarried limestone and an earthen west wing across Turkey Creek in the mid-1890s — the first such settler-built system in western Oklahoma. The reservoir and canals watered about 1,500 acres. After Fullerton's death in 1916 the works were sold to satisfy creditors. The 1919 flood broke the dam permanently; NRHP nomination text says the heavy rock sections settled and the new owners abandoned the project. Stone ruins remain and were listed on the National Register in 1976.
incidents.status: historical / ruins on the National Register; not rebuilt
incidents.notes: Exact calendar day in 1919 not given. Not the USACE Fullerton Dam in Orange County, California.

incidents.location_label: Calaveras Reservoir dam site, Calaveras Valley, California
incidents.river_or_facility: Calaveras Dam, Arroyo Hondo / Calaveras Creek
incidents.cause_summary: Hydraulic-fill construction left a weak, consolidating inner pool. The upstream shell slid into the reservoir in 1918 (static liquefaction / construction slide). Outlet tower destroyed.
incidents.what_happened: The first Calaveras Dam, begun in 1913 by Spring Valley Water Company using hydraulic fill, suffered a collapse of the upstream slope in 1918. UC Davis / California DSOD photo archive: the upstream shell slid into the reservoir and the outlet tower was destroyed. A second earthfill dam (then the world's largest) was completed in 1925 and later replaced 2014-2019 for seismic reasons.
incidents.status: first dam abandoned after slide; 1925 replacement itself replaced 2019

incidents.name: Tigra Dam
incidents.location_label: Sank River about 23 km from Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh, India
incidents.river_or_facility: Tigra Dam
incidents.cause_summary: The masonry dam failed by infiltration through its sandstone foundations on the afternoon of 19 August 1917.
incidents.what_happened: Tigra Dam on the Sank River near Gwalior, opened 1916, failed on the afternoon of 19 August 1917 when water infiltrated the sandstone foundation. incidents.name: Mammoth Dam (Gooseberry Creek)
incidents.location_label: Gooseberry Creek, about 80 miles southeast of Salt Lake City, Utah, United States
incidents.geo_source: ASDSO incident record UT00000-205 latitude 39.7157 longitude -111.299
incidents.river_or_facility: Mammoth Dam (Gooseberry Creek)
incidents.cause_summary: The unfinished earthfill-over-concrete-core dam was storing water without State Engineer approval. The upstream coffer piped, a 30 ft section of unreinforced core wall toppled, and the downstream shell washed away.
incidents.what_happened: At about 13:00 on 24 June 1917 the watchman found Mammoth Dam piping through its upstream coffer and overtopping the incomplete concrete core wall. The caretaker could not operate the intake gates. The dam fully breached and released about 11,000 acre-feet down Gooseberry Creek / Price River. The Denver & Rio Grande main line, homes, bridges and mines were damaged (about $1.2 million in 1917). ASDSO and USBR report no direct fatalities (one young sightseer later died when a car backed into the flood). The dam was never rebuilt; Scofield Reservoir later replaced the storage.
incidents.status: historical / never rebuilt; Lower Gooseberry reservoir now sits about 0.5 mile upstream
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: warning given; railroad and coal-mine shutdown until the line was repaired

sources.label: USBR — Scofield Project history (Mammoth Dam failure)

incidents.owner_operator: Price River Irrigation Company / Irrigated Lands Co.

incidents.name: Desná Dam (Bílá Desná / Burst Dam)
incidents.location_label: Bílá Desná river, Desná, Czech Republic (then Austria-Hungary)
incidents.river_or_facility: Desná Dam (Bílá Desná / Burst Dam)
incidents.cause_summary: The dam burst ten months after approval. Later geotechnical work found insufficient survey of compressible, permeable layers and an excessive hydraulic gradient.
incidents.what_happened: On 18 September 1916, about 15:30, loggers saw leakage through the new Desná dam, approved 18 November 1915. The keeper ordered draining but leakage increased. Desná was warned at 16:00; at 16:15 the dam burst, releasing about 250,000 m3. Commonly cited deaths are 62-65; 2016 research from court papers found 65 plus 2 later hospital deaths (67). Senior supervisor Karel Podhajský died by suicide. The ruins are a Czech cultural monument.
incidents.status: historical / destroyed; ruins preserved as a monument
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: hundreds in Desná lost homes
incidents.notes: Commonly cited figure 65 (court documents). Original contemporary count 62; Nývltová 2016 adds 2 later hospital deaths (67). Use 65; range 62-67.
incidents.investigating_agency: Austro-Hungarian / later Czechoslovak courts; 1996 SG Geotechnika study

incidents.name: Lake Toxaway Dam
incidents.location_label: Lake Toxaway, Transylvania County, North Carolina, United States
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Lake Toxaway 35.1345063°N 82.9407895°W (lake centroid; 1916 earthen dam at the outlet)
incidents.river_or_facility: Lake Toxaway Dam
incidents.cause_summary: The earthen dam had no water-level control. After 24 inches of rain in 24 hours on the Toxaway River the dam gave way.
incidents.what_happened: On 13 August 1916, after about 24 inches of rain in 24 hours, the 60 ft high, 500 ft long earthen dam completed in 1902 for E. H. Jennings's Toxaway Inn resort failed, sending more than 5 billion US gallons over Toxaway Falls into South Carolina. Local histories record no human deaths (one mule). The inn survived but closed; the lake was restored in the 1960s.
incidents.status: historical / dam rebuilt 1960s; lake restored as a private reservoir
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Toxaway Inn resort closed after losing the lake
incidents.notes: Sources explicitly report no human fatalities.
incidents.volume_released: more than 5 billion US gallons (about 19 million m3)

incidents.name: John Thompson's Mill Dam (Barren Creek / Thompson's Mill)
incidents.location_label: Barren Creek near New Tazewell, Claiborne County, Tennessee

incidents.river_or_facility: John Thompson's Mill Dam, Barren Creek
incidents.cause_summary: ASDSO: spillway deficiency after about 9 inches of rain in five hours. The Tennessee Historical Commission marker says record rainfall caused Thompson's Mill Dam to fail and destroy five other dams on Barren Creek.
incidents.what_happened: On 3 August 1916 (ASDSO incident date 2 August) record rain failed John Thompson's Mill Dam on Barren Creek. incidents.name: Lookout Shoals Dam (earth abutment / west wing)
incidents.location_label: Lookout Shoals Dam on the Catawba River near Catawba, North Carolina
incidents.geo_source: named Catawba, North Carolina town centroid; dam is a few miles from Catawba on the Catawba River
incidents.river_or_facility: Lookout Shoals Dam, Catawba River
incidents.cause_summary: July 1916 Great Flood / remnant of two hurricanes. Floodwaters cracked the dam and washed away about 400 feet of earth and a concrete abutment on the western / right wing beyond the spillway. The main concrete section stood.
incidents.what_happened: During the Great Flood of July 1916 the Catawba River rose about 45 feet above low water. Contemporaneous accounts: a huge crack formed in Lookout Shoals Dam; about 400 feet of earth and a concrete abutment on one side washed away (about $500,000 damage). The transformer station was submerged. Duke Energy later described the dam as partially washed away. The main 86-foot concrete structure stood and the plant was later restored.

incidents.name: Osfallet / Osfalldammen
incidents.location_label: Åmot kommune, Østerdalen, Norway
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Osfallet kraftverk infobox 61°12′06″N 11°30′23″E (present station; 1916 dam near this site; Nydammen ~600 m upstream)
incidents.river_or_facility: Søndre Osa (Glomma / Rena system); Osfallet kraftverk intake dam
incidents.cause_summary: Sudden warm weather, snowmelt and heavy rain filled the dam. Bottom gates could not be opened. International Water Power: first Norwegian buttress dam, breached after two years. Contemporary accounts also describe a cofferdam of the power-dam failing in the same flood.
incidents.what_happened: Norway's first slab/buttress (platedam) intake dam, completed 1914, failed during a spring flood on the night of 11 May 1916. Staff could not open the bottom gates or free the log chute. The flood took the machinist's house; one person in the dam-keeper house was killed. Power production for the Rena cardboard mill stopped. A replacement concrete dam (Nydammen) was built ~600 m upstream in 1916–17.
incidents.status: historic_failure; plant later rebuilt (present station 1956/1981)

sources.label: Wikipedia Osfallet kraftverk (cites NVE photo-archive 'Katastrofalt dambrudd i 1916')
International Water Power — Taking stock of Norway's dams (first buttress dam 1914, breached after two years)

incidents.owner_operator: Then associated with Rena kartongfabrikk / Osfallet kraftverk; later Eidsiva / Hafslund Kraft

incidents.name: Sweetwater Dam
incidents.location_label: Sweetwater River at Sweetwater Reservoir, San Diego County, California, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Sweetwater Dam
incidents.cause_summary: The masonry arch-gravity dam was overtopped by about 3.5 ft on 30 January 1916 when inflow reached about 45,500 cfs, far above spillway capacity. Both abutments breached and about two-thirds of the reservoir drained; the main dam body survived.
incidents.what_happened: In the same January 1916 San Diego floods that destroyed Lower Otay, Sweetwater Dam was overtopped. Peak flow on the Sweetwater was about 45,500 cfs on 30 January; water stood an estimated 3.5 ft over the crest. The north abutment then the south end beside the spillway failed, draining about two-thirds of the reservoir. Downstream damage included more than 15,000 ft of pipeline plus railway and electric lines. No sourced deaths at this dam. Rebuilt with additional spillway capacity and still in use.
incidents.status: rebuilt after 1916 abutment failures; still in service (Sweetwater Authority)
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: downstream Sweetwater Valley infrastructure destroyed (pipeline, railway, utilities)
incidents.notes: Wikipedia list dates the event 1916-01-27 (start of the flood sequence); peak overtopping described as 30 January 1916. Sources report 0 fatalities at Sweetwater.
incidents.owner_operator: San Diego Land and Town Company / later Sweetwater Authority
incidents.breach_size: both abutments failed; main dam body survived

incidents.name: Lower Otay Dam
incidents.location_label: Otay River / Lower Otay Reservoir, San Diego County, California, United States
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Lower Otay Reservoir 32.6372°N 116.9249°W (present Savage Dam; 1897 rockfill dam was at this reservoir)
incidents.river_or_facility: Lower Otay Dam
incidents.cause_summary: The 125 ft rockfill dam was overtopped in the January 1916 San Diego floods after days of extreme rain. Courts later treated the event as an act of God; local blame of rainmaker Charles Hatfield was not upheld.
incidents.what_happened: On 27 January 1916 the original Lower Otay rockfill dam (built 1897) failed during the record San Diego County floods. A wall of water 20-100 ft high swept Otay Valley, killing more than 14 people and destroying farms and buildings, including the Montgomery residence at Fruitland. The present Savage Dam (arch-gravity, 1918) replaced it.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Otay Valley farms and buildings swept away

incidents.name: Lyman Dam
incidents.location_label: Little Colorado River about 11-12 miles upstream of St. Johns, Arizona
incidents.geo_source: HMDB Lyman Dam marker at Lyman Lake State Park entrance (34°21.704′N, 109°23.139′W)
incidents.river_or_facility: Lyman Dam, Little Colorado River
incidents.cause_summary: ASDSO: sudden piping of the homogeneous clay embankment near the maximum section. Post-failure work pointed to reservoir pressure transmitted through coarse foundation deposits and rapid erosion of soft Chinle-derived clays.
incidents.what_happened: Lyman Dam, an 800-foot-long, 65-foot-high homogeneous clay embankment completed 1911-13 without foundation cutoffs or drains, failed suddenly at 22:45 on 14 April 1915. Observers described a rush of water at the base followed by a 30-foot rise on the downstream face and a breach that opened to about 350 feet. The flood drowned eight people (two women and six children).
incidents.status: rebuilt with State of Arizona loans; later rehabilitated; Lyman Lake State Park occupies the site

sources.label: New York Times — Dam Breaks; 8 Drowned (16 April 1915)

incidents.notes: NYT dateline says the dam gave way shortly before 01:00 on 15 April; ASDSO gives 22:45 on 14 April. Eight deaths are consistent across ASDSO, NYT and the state marker.
incidents.breach_size: gap about 350 feet long (ASDSO account)
incidents.investigating_agency: post-failure investigations cited by ASDSO; reconstruction investigations 1916-22

incidents.name: Hatchtown Dam
incidents.location_label: Sevier River at the junction of Asay and Mammoth creeks, south of Hatch, Utah, United States
incidents.geo_source: Hatch, Utah town centroid; dam stood at the Asay/Mammoth/Sevier junction about 20 miles above Panguitch (Salt Lake Tribune 26-27 May 1914)

incidents.cause_summary: Piping along the rubble-masonry / concrete outlet culvert. Contributing factors cited by later ASDSO review: no cutoff collars, poor foundation along the core trench, an old culvert left from the 1903 dam, and unfilled exploration pits.
incidents.what_happened: On 25 May 1914 the state-built Hatchtown earth dam on the upper Sevier failed after afternoon slides and seepage along the outlet tunnel. A roughly 120-140 ft breach released about 12,000-14,000 acre-feet. Couriers and telephone warnings (notably Rosalia Whitaker at Circleville) cleared the valley. The flood wrecked ranches and Circleville; Piute Reservoir absorbed the wave and held. No confirmed deaths. A first dam at the site had already failed on 19 May 1903.
incidents.status: historical / not rebuilt as Hatchtown; later Sevier storage is elsewhere
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Circleville and ranches along ~50-70 miles of the Sevier; 15+ homes swept; 75-300 people displaced

incidents.name: Broken Down Dam (Fergus Falls City Light Station)
incidents.location_label: Otter Tail River above Fergus Falls, Minnesota, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Broken Down Dam (Fergus Falls City Light Station)
incidents.cause_summary: The concrete gravity hydro dam was built on natural springs without adequate site investigation; spring flow undermined the foundations within a year of first operation.

incidents.name: Hauser Dam (first steel dam)
incidents.location_label: Missouri River about 14 miles northeast of Helena, Montana, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Hauser Dam (first steel dam)

Telegrams and a Great Northern locomotive warned towns downstream; Craig was evacuated and Great Falls saw only about a 7 ft rise. No fatalities are recorded. Damages were estimated at more than $1 million. A concrete gravity dam was completed on the site in 1911.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Craig and other Missouri River settlements evacuated; Holter construction camp swept away

incidents.name: Austin Dam (Great Granite Dam / Lake McDonald)
incidents.location_label: Colorado River near Austin, Texas, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Austin Dam (Great Granite Dam / Lake McDonald)
incidents.cause_summary: A roughly 60 ft masonry dam built across the Balcones Fault Zone slid on its foundation after a flood put more than 11 ft of water over the crest. USGS contemporaneous report describes two about 250 ft sections shoved about 60 ft downstream without overturning.
incidents.what_happened: At 11:20 on 7 April 1900, after about 17 inches of rain in 48 hours and roughly 11 ft of overflow, a section of Austin's granite masonry dam about 300 ft from the east end gave way. Two sections each about 250 ft long slid 60-80 ft downstream. The current wrecked the powerhouse. USGS engineer Thomas U. Taylor recorded five employees and three boys drowned there. Lake McDonald emptied and Austin lost electric power for months. Later replaced by Tom Miller Dam in the 1940s.
incidents.status: historical / destroyed; replaced by Tom Miller Dam (1940s)
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Austin left without electrical power for months

incidents.name: Bouzey Dam (réservoir de Bouzey)
incidents.location_label: Avière valley at Bouzey, near Chaumousey / Épinal, Vosges, France
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Lac de Bouzey 48°09′52″N 6°21′22″E (rebuilt reservoir on the same site)
incidents.river_or_facility: Bouzey Dam (réservoir de Bouzey)
incidents.cause_summary: Masonry gravity dam on porous sandstone. A 1884 first-filling slide (about 35 cm downstream) left the profile cracked. On 27 April 1895 excessive uplift inside the masonry opened a roughly 170 m breach about 10 m below the water surface. Maurice Lévy's 1895 Académie des Sciences note made uplift a standard design load.
incidents.what_happened: The masonry Canal de l'Est feeder dam on the Avière failed suddenly around dawn, releasing nearly 7 million m3. The flood destroyed the hamlet of Bouzey and tore through Uxegney, Domèvre, Oncourt, Frizon and Nomexy before entering the Moselle. Engineering summaries and La Revue EIN give 87 dead. The dam had already suffered a major first-filling displacement in March 1884 and had been patched rather than rebuilt. It was reconstructed with a lowered water level in 1900-1901 and again in 1939.
incidents.status: rebuilt (1900-1901, 1939); present reservoir still feeds the Canal des Vosges
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Bouzey hamlet destroyed; Domèvre 28 houses and 32 dead; Nomexy 8 dead; railway and canal damaged

incidents.name: Clear Lake Dam (Eldred and Thompson mill dam, Spartansburg)
incidents.location_label: Clear Lake / East Branch Oil Creek, Spartansburg, Pennsylvania
incidents.river_or_facility: Clear Lake Dam on East Branch Oil Creek
incidents.cause_summary: An earthen mill dam at Spartansburg failed after extreme rain on 4–5 June 1892; the surge down Oil Creek wrecked oil works in Titusville and Oil City and set the flood on fire.
incidents.what_happened: After a day of cloudbursts (local estimates near 10 inches at Spartansburg), the earthen mill dam of Thompson and Eldred at Clear Lake failed shortly after midnight on 5 June 1892. ASDSO's incident record (PA00175) dates the overtopping failure 11:30 p.m. and notes about 10 similar headwater dams also failed. The wave ran down East Branch Oil Creek into Titusville and then Oil City, rupturing tanks so that oil, naphtha and gas rode the flood and ignited. NWS's 125th-anniversary summary puts the death toll at about 126 (about 72 in Titusville, 54 in Oil City), second in Pennsylvania flood deaths only to Johnstown 1889. The dam was later rebuilt (1905) as a concrete gravity structure.
incidents.status: historical / reconstructed 1905 as concrete gravity Clear Lake Dam
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Titusville business district largely destroyed by flood and fire; Oil City also burned

incidents.name: Walnut Grove Dam
incidents.location_label: Hassayampa River north of Wickenburg, Arizona, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Walnut Grove Dam
incidents.cause_summary: A rockfill dam with an undersized spillway (final roughly 26 by 7 ft, about 2,200 cfs) was overtopped by an estimated 25-year flood after days of rain. Construction had been repeatedly cheapened; a messenger sent to warn downstream camps got drunk and never delivered the warning.
incidents.what_happened: After about 7 inches of rain from 16 February 1890, Walnut Grove Dam on the Hassayampa River overtopped about 21:00 on 21 February and failed shortly after midnight on 22 February. About 4 billion gallons rushed down the canyon, destroying the diversion-dam workers' camp and settlements toward Wickenburg. Commonly cited deaths exceed 100; some accounts put the toll as high as 150. The dam was never rebuilt.
incidents.status: historical / not rebuilt; remnants of spillway and diversion tunnel remain
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: workers' camp and downstream Hassayampa settlements destroyed

Modifications that lowered the crest, clogged the spillway with fish screens and removed discharge pipes reduced freeboard and outlet capacity.
