incidents.name: Fergoug / Habra Dam (1881 breach)
incidents.location_label: Barrage de Fergoug on Oued el Hammam / Habra, north of Mohammadia, Algeria
incidents.river_or_facility: Barrage de Fergoug (Barrage de l'Habra) on Oued el Hammam / Habra
incidents.cause_summary: A masonry gravity dam built with porous local stone and expansive lime cement was overtopped by about 3.9 m during a December cloudburst; the air-side face then failed over 125 m.
incidents.what_happened: The first Habra / Fergoug masonry dam, built 1865–1873 above Perrégaux (now Mohammadia) to irrigate the Habra–Macta plain, had already lost its spillway during construction on 10 March 1872. German Wikipedia, citing contemporary Austrian press, says mid-December 1881 storms dropped about 170 mm of rain; inflow of roughly 850 m³/s overtopped the 36–43 m wall by a calculated 3.9 m and about 98 million m³ passed the crest in one night. Inferior sandstone and cement left the masonry porous. The wall broke over 125 m. Fatality estimates are 200–250 (some contemporary reports 350–400). The new colonial town of Perrégaux was wrecked, with houses, bridges and railway track destroyed. The dam was rebuilt 1883–1885.
incidents.status: Rebuilt 1883–1885; that second wall failed again in 1927.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Perrégaux / Mohammadia town flooded; number of displaced not stated in sources fetched
incidents.notes: Deaths left at 250, the figure German Wikipedia uses as the main estimate; contemporary reports also gave 200 and 350–400.
incidents.breach_size: about 125 m of the masonry wall
incidents.downstream_risk: Perrégaux (Mohammadia) and the Habra plain

incidents.name: Lynde Brook Reservoir Dam (Worcester water supply)
incidents.location_label: Lynde Brook Reservoir, Leicester, Massachusetts
incidents.geo_source: NID / DamLookup Lynde Brook Reservoir Dam 42.25021, -71.87381
incidents.river_or_facility: Lynde Brook Reservoir Dam
incidents.cause_summary: Known leakage through the rebuilt earthen water-supply dam progressed to a breach on 30 March 1876, emptying hundreds of millions of gallons into the Lynde Brook valley.
incidents.what_happened: Worcester's Lynde Brook Reservoir dam, first built in 1863 and raised in 1872–73, had leaked for years. After the 1874 Mill River disaster, local alarm rose, but the leaks were not cured. On 30 March 1876 the dam gave way in the late afternoon, releasing on the order of 760 million gallons. The flood wrecked mills in Cherry Valley (Leicester/Worcester), took out about 500 ft of Boston & Albany track, and damaged houses. Warnings kept the death toll at zero. New England Water Works Association history estimates about $750,000 damage. Worcester rebuilt the dam; the site is still a city water-supply reservoir.
incidents.status: historical / rebuilt; still a Worcester water-supply dam
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Cherry Valley, Webster Square and Jamesville mill districts

incidents.name: Langley Lake Dam (Union Bay)
incidents.region: Union Bay, Vancouver Island, British Columbia
incidents.location_label: Langley Lake above Union Bay, Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada
incidents.geo_source: BC Dam Safety case note: dam 6.4 km upstream of Union Bay (49.585°N 124.886°W)
incidents.river_or_facility: Langley Lake timber-crib dam; pipeline to Canada Collieries plant
incidents.cause_summary: A poorly connected timber-crib/earthfill dam of reversed-arch plan, built of uncompacted surface scrapings, failed after heavy rain raised the reservoir and debris blocked a flashboarded spillway.
incidents.what_happened: About 17:00 on 10 February 1912 a 52 m section of the 6.6 m timber-crib dam on Langley Lake, 6.4 km upstream of Union Bay, pivoted open like a door. BC Dam Safety, excerpting Mitchell (Engineering News, 1912), says the dam had been built about 1908 to supply Canada Collieries' coal-washing plant; the earth fill was 'wretched surface scrapings' and the four straight crib sections formed an arch that bulged out of the reservoir. Heavy rain had raised the reservoir to the crest; flashboards were not pulled and debris blocked the narrow spillway opening. A 3.3 m wall of water and debris slammed into Union Bay, washed workers' shacks into the bay (some caught fire) and destroyed other buildings. One person drowned. Property loss was estimated at $50,000 (1912). BC Dam Safety calls this the only fatality on record for Canadian dam failures in that case note.
incidents.status: Dam destroyed; town rebuilt. Contemporary report blamed 'inexcusable ignorance and carelessness'.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: scores of workers' shacks washed out; Union Bay Chinatown and industrial buildings destroyed (U of T disaster compilation: 45 houses)

incidents.cause_summary: After a process-filter failure, improvised descending ponds and a coal-cake dump were used as containment; the makeshift system failed and slurry entered Collins Gulch.
incidents.what_happened: On 24 August 2013 coal slurry from Coalmont Energy's Basin Mine poured into Collins Gulch and the Tulameen River, turning the river black for days. Two managers pleaded guilty in September 2017 to introducing waste and were fined about $10,000 each for the Habitat Conservation Trust Foundation. Court heard later testing showed no or very limited impact on fish habitat. No source fetched reported deaths.

incidents.what_happened: In 1974 the Clinton Creek waste-rock dump at Cassiar Asbestos's mine (1968–1978) failed as a lateral spread, blocking about 700 m of Clinton Creek and forming 25 m-deep Hudgeon Lake. incidents.status: Abandoned; federal remediation underway. Hudgeon Lake still impounded behind waste rock.

incidents.what_happened: Haldon Dam, a ~15–20 m zoned earthfill irrigation dam holding about 250,000 m³ on Starborough Creek (which flows through Seddon), was damaged in the July–August 2013 Cook Strait earthquake sequence. RNZ (July 2013): owner Richard Bell began emptying the dam after cracks; Marlborough District Council called a second independent inspection. NZGS remediation paper: crest and upstream shoulder suffered serious damage; the regulator enforced a 5.5 m emergency lowering (spillway weir demolished, outlet trench cut) because a failure could have sent about 120 m³/s through Seddon. Construction had a history of non-compliance. The dam did not breach. Official NZ dam-incident series records no fatalities.
incidents.status: Emergency drawdown; later two-stage remediation to a compliant lowered reservoir.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Seddon (~12 km downstream) was the at-risk community; no breach

incidents.region: Edgecumbe, Bay of Plenty, North Island

incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Edgecumbe 37.975°S 176.825°E; breach at College Road
incidents.river_or_facility: Rangitāiki River Scheme stopbank / concrete floodwall at College Road
incidents.cause_summary: Independent review: 1973 foundation placement, unrepaired 1987 Edgecumbe-earthquake foundation damage, and a 2012 concrete pad allowed piping/pressure to collapse the wall; incomplete Reid's Floodway upgrades left Edgecumbe exposed.
incidents.what_happened: At about 08:30 on 6 April 2017 the Rangitāiki River breached the College Road stopbank/floodwall at Edgecumbe during remnants of Cyclone Debbie. Independent review (Cullen, Christensen, Price) for Bay of Plenty Regional Council: no loss of life; 15 houses permanently uninhabitable and more than 250 needing long repairs; about 1,600–2,000 residents evacuated. Mayor Tony Bonne told RNZ the bank collapsed rather than overtopped. The panel later found faulty 1973 foundations, 1987 earthquake damage never fixed in the foundation, and a 2012 concrete pad that increased pressure. Incomplete Reid's Floodway works likely left more water on the town. Matahina Dam releases reduced downstream levels but probably would not have prevented the breach.
incidents.status: Review published Oct 2017; scheme upgrades followed.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 1,600–2,000 Edgecumbe residents evacuated

incidents.name: Matahina Dam (Edgecumbe earthquake)
incidents.region: Rangitāiki River, Bay of Plenty, North Island
incidents.location_label: Matahina Dam, Rangitāiki River, New Zealand
incidents.river_or_facility: Matahina earth-rockfill dam and power station
incidents.cause_summary: The M6.3 Edgecumbe earthquake shook the 80–86 m dam (crest PGA 0.42 g); later investigations found core cracking and internal erosion that forced a second drawdown and repairs.
incidents.what_happened: At 13:42 on 2 March 1987 the M6.3 Edgecumbe earthquake shook Matahina Dam, about 23 km from the epicentre. Gillon (Ministry of Works): crest rockfill settled about 100 mm and moved 250 mm downstream; crest acceleration 0.42 g; lake drawn down 2.5 m as a precaution (downstream residents unofficially evacuated on the falling river). No major leakage immediately. Later ISSMGE/NZSEE work: a large cavity upstream of the core on the right abutment, continued settlement, and in December 1987 active internal erosion at the left abutment forced another lowering and major core/abutment repairs. The dam did not breach. Official NZ dam-incident series records no fatalities.
incidents.status: Repaired 1987–88; still operating.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: unofficial downstream evacuation after the first drawdown (Gillon)

incidents.name: Arapuni Dam headrace (1930 crack and dewatering)
incidents.region: Waikato River, south of Hamilton, North Island
incidents.location_label: Arapuni Dam and headrace, Waikato River, New Zealand
incidents.river_or_facility: Arapuni concrete gravity dam and headrace canal, Waikato River
incidents.cause_summary: A large crack opened in the headrace near the powerhouse as nontronite clay infill eroded in ignimbrite foundation fissures; the reservoir was fully dewatered.
incidents.what_happened: In June 1930, about a year after first power, a large crack opened in the Arapuni headrace near the powerhouse. Engineering NZ heritage record and Papers Past (Otago Daily Times, 11 June 1930): a diver found a vertical fracture leaking into adjoining country; the headrace was emptied, the river returned to the diversion tunnel, and the station shut until April 1932. The main dam was reported unaffected. Swedish experts recommended an impervious headrace lining and a grout curtain at the upstream heel — the start of a seepage history that continued (see 2000 piping record). No source fetched reported deaths.
incidents.status: Returned to service April 1932 after lining and grout curtain.

incidents.name: Arapuni Dam foundation piping (2000–2002)
incidents.region: Waikato River, south of Hamilton, North Island

incidents.river_or_facility: Arapuni Dam foundation / drainage system
incidents.cause_summary: Erosion of nontronite clay infill in an ignimbrite fracture formed a pipe from the reservoir into the dam drainage system.
incidents.what_happened: ISSMGE/NZGS papers on Arapuni: in 2000 a trend of rising pressure and flow was identified and solid particles of clay and bitumen, plus lake life, exited the drainage system. Mighty River Power / DamWatch showed nontronite infill had eroded from a fracture, piping the reservoir to the drains. The pipe was grouted in 2002. Earlier (1995) exploratory holes had hit high-pressure seepage, grouted in December 2001. The dam did not breach. Official NZ dam-incident series records no fatalities. Later discrete concrete cut-off panels were built through the ignimbrite.

incidents.what_happened: On 13–14 February 2023 Cyclone Gabrielle delivered 300–350 mm on the Tūtaekurī/Ngaruroro catchments. incidents.river_or_facility: Scales Pond Dam, Dunk River
incidents.cause_summary: P.E.I. Environment said rains and rapid snowmelt contributed to failure of the unused former mill/hydro dam, which burst a ~12 m hole and drained the pond into the Dunk River.
incidents.what_happened: On Saturday 4 April 2009 the dam at Scales Pond, just east of Summerside on the Dunk River, burst. A P.E.I. Environment, Energy and Forestry release dated 6 April 2009 (the following Monday) said the dam failed Saturday, sending a large volume of water, ice and silt into the Dunk River, and that rains and rapid snowmelt were believed to have contributed. CBC, reporting the same weekend, said the unused former hydro dam left a gaping hole about 12 metres wide; ice and water toppled 9–12 m trees; silt raised concern for salmon and trout spawning; and the pond, a long-standing recreation and fishing spot, drained within hours. The same department said the pond began as an early-19th-century mill pond, powered a hydro station in the 1920s, and became a trout-fishing site in the 1930s. CBC later reported the dam washed away in the 2009 spring flood and that a new concrete dam with a fish ladder was completed in 2013 after a ~$1 million community-led rebuild.
incidents.status: Rebuilt as a concrete dam with fish ladder; pond restored 2013.

incidents.what_happened: The Government of New Brunswick flood history for 25–26 October 1933 describes a heavy autumn rainfall in southern New Brunswick (77.7 mm at Fredericton, 91.2 mm at Sussex, 124.5 mm at Rexton) that turned the Kennebecasis valley 'a veritable sea of water from Penobsquis to Hampton and throughout the Millstream district.' incidents.cause_summary: Fraser freshet overtopped neglected wooden-frame/earth dykes; Wikipedia and the Chilliwack Progress date a major Semiault Creek dyke break to 28 May 1948.
incidents.what_happened: During the 1948 Fraser River freshet, the Semiault Creek dyke at Chilliwack broke on 28 May. Wikipedia (Fraser River) lists that date as the first of a sequence of named lower-valley dyke failures. The Chilliwack Progress, citing the Chilliwack Museum's flood history, says that on 28 May the Mission gauge reached 23.05 feet (7 m) and there was a major break in the Semiault dike, which was soon repaired; later small breaks occurred again as the Cannor dyke failed. The Weather Network's 1948 anniversary piece also dates the Semiault Creek dike break to Friday 28 May, before the Glendale and Cannor failures already recorded separately. Legion Magazine published a Chilliwack Museum photograph of volunteers repairing the dike on Semiault Creek, a Fraser tributary. Regional 1948 deaths (often given as 10) are not copied onto this named dyke.
incidents.status: Repaired in 1948; Fraser Valley dykes later widened and heightened.

incidents.name: Moutoa floodway southern stopbank (trestle bridge)
incidents.region: Moutoa Basin / Horowhenua, Manawatū-Whanganui, North Island
incidents.location_label: Southern stopbank of the Moutoa floodway at the trestle bridge, below Ōpiki, New Zealand
incidents.geo_source: LINZ Moutoa Floodway −40.510417, 175.324972 (NZMS260 S24); breach at an unnamed trestle on the southern stopbank, not necessarily the SH1 Whirokino trestle
incidents.river_or_facility: Moutoa floodway southern stopbank, Lower Manawatū Scheme
incidents.cause_summary: Court of Appeal (Easton Agriculture, 2013): after the Moutoa sluice gates were opened, the southern floodway stopbank failed at a trestle bridge; the Sutherland review blamed the bridge–stopbank interaction.
incidents.what_happened: On 16 February 2004 Horizons (then Manawatu-Wanganui Regional Council) opened the Moutoa sluice gates at 07:00 to relieve the Manawatū River. The New Zealand Court of Appeal in Easton Agriculture Ltd v Manawatu-Wanganui Regional Council [2013] NZCA 79 found that during the night of 16–17 February the southern stopbank of the Moutoa floodway failed at a trestle bridge: a farmer saw an upstream breach about 03:20 on 17 February; further breaches were seen at 05:30; and at 06:30 a 'catastrophic' blow-out occurred downstream of the bridge. The breach reached 23 m upstream and 17 m downstream of the bridge centreline; the bridge itself stayed intact. Floodwater covered the Moutoa Basin and the appellants' farms for about 12 days. The council's Sutherland Report said the likely cause was interaction between the bridge structure and the stopbank. Te Ara records that the February 2004 flood was the largest on the Manawatū since 1902 and that a number of Lower Manawatū Scheme stopbank failures inundated about 25% of the protected area. No source attached a death count to this breach.
incidents.status: Stopbank repaired; scheme upgrades after 2004.

incidents.name: Matahina Dam (1967 first-filling cavity)
incidents.region: Rangitāiki River, Bay of Plenty, North Island
incidents.location_label: Matahina Dam right abutment, Rangitāiki River, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Matahina Power Station 38.114°S 176.814°E (same dam as the 1987 earthquake incident, different event)
incidents.river_or_facility: Matahina Dam, Rangitāiki River
incidents.cause_summary: First filling cracked the core and inner transition against an unremoved abutment bench; a pipe developed and an erosion cavity appeared on the downstream right abutment.
incidents.what_happened: Matahina, a rockfill dam with a rolled silt core on the Rangitāiki, was filled in late 1966–early 1967. ISSMGE (Gillon and Newton, citing Galloway 1967): after the lake was held on the spillway at RL 66 m, filling from 5 January raised the lake to RL 74.7 m in six days and to RL 76.2 m on 22 January; large leakage then appeared in the underdrain. About two weeks later a subsidence was found on the downstream side of the core at the right abutment. A shaft 8.5 × 6.1 m in plan was taken 16.5 m down to RL 63 m and revealed a 1.8 m construction bench at RL 67.4 m that had not been removed, plus a 200 mm pipe into the downstream rockfill; material loss was estimated at more than 100 m³. International Water Power and Wikipedia describe the same first-filling cavity, lake lowering, and core repair with a plastic-concrete patch and filter backfill. The repair performed until the separate 2 March 1987 Edgecumbe earthquake incident (already drafted). Engineering papers and the official NZ dam-incident series record no fatalities.
